title: Episode 266: Charles Lindbergh: The Spirit of St. Louis, 33.5 Hours to Paris, and the Lone Eagle
description:
The electrifying, tragic, and historic life of Charles Augustus Lindbergh: the shy twenty-five-year-old airmail pilot from Minnesota who conquered the Atlantic Ocean in thirty-three and a half hours of solitary flight. Competing for the twenty-five-thousand-dollar Orteig Prize in May 1927, Lindbergh designed the custom single-engine Ryan monoplane 'Spirit of St. Louis', stripping out parachutes, radio, and front windshield to maximize fuel capacity. Taking off from a muddy Roosevelt Field on Long Island, Lindbergh battled fog, sleet, hallucinations, and deadly fatigue to land at Le Bourget field in Paris, greeted by one hundred and fifty thousand hysterical spectators in the first global media frenzy in human history. Enduring the horrific kidnapping and murder of his infant son in 1932, controversial pre-war isolationism, and secret combat missions in the Pacific, Lindbergh remains the immortal Lone Eagle of the skies.

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, our Top 50 Famous Non-President Americans series chronicles the flight that shrank the globe: a solitary twenty-five-year-old airmail pilot who flew alone across thirty-six hundred miles of stormy ocean into immortality. Here is George with the life of Charles Lindbergh.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE BARNSTORMER OF LITTLE FALLS: 1902 TO 1926
Born in Detroit in February 1902 and raised on a farm along the Mississippi River in Little Falls, Minnesota, Charles Augustus Lindbergh Jr. was the son of a fiery, anti-war populist United States congressman and a high school chemistry teacher. From childhood, 'Slim' was an introspective, mechanically gifted youth who loved tinkering with Model T engines and roaming the outdoors. Dropping out of the University of Wisconsin's engineering program in 1922, Lindbergh enrolled in the Nebraska Aircraft Corporation's flying school in Lincoln, learning to fly an antiquated World War I Curtiss JN-4 'Jenny' biplane. He spent two wild, perilous years as a barnstormer across the Midwest, performing daredevil wing-walking, parachute jumps, and stunt flying at county fairs. In 1924, Lindbergh enlisted in the United States Army Air Service at Brooks Field in Texas, graduating top of his class as a pursuit pilot and surviving two mid-air collisions by parachuting to safety, earning entry into the elite Caterpillar Club. In 1926, Lindbergh became the chief airmail pilot for the Robertson Aircraft Corporation, flying the dangerous nighttime route between St. Louis and Chicago in open-cockpit de Havilland biplanes through blinding blizzards and summer thunderstorms, twice bailing out into pitch-black farm fields when running out of fuel in dense fog.  Young Charles' solitary excursions along the pine-forested banks of the Mississippi River instilled in him an extraordinary self-reliance and emotional composure that never cracked under pressure. His daredevil barnstorming years across the prairie states taught him to read weather patterns from the cockpit and handle sudden engine failures over unfamiliar terrain.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE ORTEIG PRIZE AND THE SPIRIT OF ST. LOUIS: 1926 TO 1927
In 1919, French-American hotelier Raymond Orteig offered a lavish twenty-five-thousand-dollar prize to the first aviator to fly non-stop between New York and Paris. By late 1926, the challenge had turned deadly: famous World War I aces and lavishly funded teams in multi-engine aircraft were crashing and dying in attempts. Rene Fonck crashed on takeoff in a massive Sikorsky biplane, burning two crewmen alive; naval hero Richard E. Byrd broke bones in trials; and French war heroes Charles Nungesser and Francois Coli vanished without a trace over the Atlantic in their biplane, The White Bird. Twenty-four-year-old Lindbergh approached the challenge with radical, minimalist logic: multi-engine planes were heavy, complex, and prone to engine failure; a light, single-engine monoplane with a reliable air-cooled radial engine offered the highest probability of success. Securing fifteen thousand dollars from a syndicate of St. Louis businessmen, Lindbergh hired Donald Hall and Ryan Airlines in San Diego to design the custom monoplane, named the 'Spirit of St. Louis'. Lindbergh ruthlessly stripped every ounce of weight: he carried no radio, no sextant, no gas gauge, no parachute, and placed the massive main fuel tank directly in front of the cockpit to protect himself in a crash—completely blocking forward vision, requiring a small periscope to see directly ahead!  Donald Hall and the skilled craftsmen at Ryan Airlines worked in shifts around the clock in an abandoned fish cannery in San Diego to fabricate the Spirit of St. Louis in just sixty days. Lindbergh's calculation that every pound of eliminated equipment allowed additional gallons of gasoline demonstrated an uncompromising engineering logic that made transatlantic flight possible.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE MUDDY RUNWAY AT ROOSEVELT FIELD: MAY 20, 1927
On May 12, 1927, Lindbergh flew the Spirit of St. Louis from San Diego to New York in record time, arriving at Curtiss and Roosevelt fields on Long Island. For a week, violent Atlantic rainstorms kept all aircraft grounded. Unable to sleep due to excitement and journalists pounding on his hotel door, Lindbergh arrived at Roosevelt Field at dawn on Friday, May 20, 1927, having been awake for over twenty-four hours. A cold, gray drizzle fell across the muddy dirt runway. The Spirit of St. Louis was loaded with four hundred and fifty-one gallons of high-octane gasoline, weighing over five thousand pounds—double its empty weight. Mechanics urged him to postpone, but Lindbergh climbed into his wicker seat, donned his leather flying helmet and goggles, and revved the two-hundred-and-twenty-three-horsepower Wright Whirlwind J-5C radial engine. At seven-fifty-two AM, the plane began its agonizingly slow crawl down the muddy runway, bouncing through puddles and barely clearing telephone wires and a tractor at the end of the field by twenty feet. The Lone Eagle was airborne, heading out over the gray, white-capped Atlantic Ocean.  The rain-slicked runway at Roosevelt Field was surrounded by thousands of anxious spectators who held their breath as the overloaded monoplane struggled to lift into the morning mist. Clearing the telephone wires at the runway's edge by barely twenty feet, Lindbergh banked toward the Long Island Sound, entering the vast solitude of the Atlantic Ocean.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: 33.5 HOURS OVER THE ABYSS: FOG, SLEET, AND HALLUCINATIONS
The thirty-three-and-a-half-hour crossing of thirty-six hundred miles was an epic ordeal of human willpower against the overwhelming physical agony of sleep deprivation. Flying by dead reckoning with only a magnetic compass, airspeed indicator, and an eight-day watch, Lindbergh skimmed ten feet above the foaming Atlantic waves to take advantage of ground effect. Passing over Nova Scotia and Newfoundland, night fell as he entered towering walls of storm clouds and freezing fog over the Grand Banks. Heavy sleet began coating the fabric wings, threatening to add fatal weight; Lindbergh had to fly blind through freezing squalls, dodging ice-laden clouds. By the eighteenth hour, sheer exhaustion overwhelmed his nervous system: his eyelids felt weighted with lead, and he was forced to hold his eyes open with his fingers, leaning his face into the freezing gale through the open cockpit window and splashing cold water on his cheeks to prevent losing consciousness. In the dark silence of the cockpit, Lindbergh experienced vivid, friendly hallucinations: he saw ghostly, translucent phantoms floating through the cockpit, whispering words of encouragement and guiding his navigational headings. At dawn, skimming over fishing fleets off the coast of Ireland, Lindbergh circled a fishing smack, throttling down his engine and shouting out the window: 'Which way is Ireland?' The stunned fisherman stood paralyzed in silence.  Flying through towering storm walls and blinding sleet over the Grand Banks, Lindbergh relied entirely on his compass and airspeed indicator, fighting the physical delirium of sleep deprivation. The friendly, translucent phantoms that populated his cockpit during the long night hours spoke to the profound psychological strain of solitary endurance at the frontier of human possibility.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE LANDING AT LE BOURGET: MAY 21, 1927
Crossing the green coastal headlands of southwestern Ireland at Dingle Bay, Lindbergh discovered to his astonishment that his dead-reckoning navigation was barely three miles off course after two thousand miles of ocean flight! Crossing the English Channel at sunset, he followed the gleaming silver ribbon of the Seine River toward the radiant glow of Paris. At ten-twenty-two PM local time on Saturday, May 21, 1927—thirty-three hours, thirty minutes, and twenty-nine seconds after leaving New York—the silver monoplane touched down gracefully on the grass runways of Le Bourget aerodrome outside Paris. Lindbergh expected a few curious mechanics; instead, an overwhelming tidal wave of one hundred and fifty thousand hysterical spectators broke through military police lines and surged toward the airplane like an unstoppable tsunami. Spectators hoisted Lindbergh onto their shoulders, cheering, weeping, and tearing fabric souvenirs from the wings, while two French aviators cleverly whisked Lindbergh away into an unmarked car to save him from being crushed to death by love. At twenty-five years old, Charles Lindbergh had become the most famous human being on planet earth.  The joyous roar of the one hundred and fifty thousand spectators at Le Bourget field broke all police barricades, celebrating the triumph of an unassuming youth who had shrunk the globe. The French government awarded Lindbergh the Legion of Honor, while crowds outside his Paris hotel chanted his name through the night in an unprecedented outpouring of international affection.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE AGONY OF FAME AND THE CRIME OF THE CENTURY: 1927 TO 1932
Returning to America aboard the cruiser USS Memphis, Lindbergh was awarded the Medal of Honor, and over four million cheering citizens showered him with eighteen hundred tons of ticker tape in New York City. In 1929, Lindbergh married Anne Morrow, the gifted daughter of the U.S. Ambassador to Mexico, pioneering global commercial airline routes together for Pan American World Airways. But global fame exacted a horrific, tragic price. On the stormy night of March 1, 1932, their twenty-month-old firstborn son, Charles Augustus Lindbergh Jr., was kidnapped from his second-floor nursery crib in their secluded home near Hopewell, New Jersey, leaving behind a crude ransom note on the radiator. For ten agonizing weeks, the entire nation followed the frantic search. Despite paying a fifty-thousand-dollar cash ransom in a Bronx cemetery, the child's battered, decomposed body was found dumped in a shallow roadside ditch two months later, having suffered a fractured skull on the night of the abduction. The 'Crime of the Century' and the sensational 1935 trial and execution of German immigrant carpenter Bruno Richard Hauptmann drove the shattered, hunted Lindbergh family into bitter self-imposed exile in England.  The ticker-tape parade in New York City showered Lindbergh with over eighteen hundred tons of paper, a rapturous welcome that overwhelmed the shy, modest Midwestern aviator. The horrifying abduction and murder of baby Charles Jr. destroyed the family's peace, exposing the toxic price of uncontrolled sensationalist media celebrity in modern America.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: CONTROVERSY, WAR, AND THE PACIFIC SKIES: THE FINAL LEGACY
In the late 1930s, Lindbergh's reputation suffered a catastrophic eclipse: touring German aircraft factories at the request of the American military, Lindbergh was awarded a civilian medal by Hermann Göring and became the charismatic public leader of the America First Committee, arguing passionately against American intervention in World War II and delivering controversial speeches that drew fierce accusations of anti-Semitism and Nazi appeasement. Following the attack on Pearl Harbor, Lindbergh immediately volunteered for service; though President Roosevelt refused to restore his military commission, Lindbergh traveled to the Pacific theater as a civilian technical consultant for United Aircraft, flying fifty unauthorized combat combat missions in P-38 Lightnings and F4U Corsairs, teaching pilots fuel-conservation techniques and shooting down a Japanese reconnaissance plane in aerial combat. In his later years, Lindbergh became a passionate conservationist, living on the remote coast of Maui, Hawaii, where he died of lymphoma in August 1974. Charles Lindbergh's life embodied the dizzying heights and tragic depths of the twentieth century: the quiet Midwestern youth whose courage, precision, and thirty-three hours of solitary grace opened the skies and united a planet.  Lindbergh's unauthorized combat missions in the Pacific theater showcased his peerless aeronautical intuition, extending the combat range of American fighters by hundreds of miles. His final years of ecological advocacy in the Pacific reflected his mature realization that technological advancement must be balanced by a deep reverence for the natural world.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories. Next week, our Top 50 Famous Non-President Americans series continues with Episode 267: Amelia Earhart—The Queen of the Air, the Transatlantic Solo, and the Mystery of Howland Island. Until then, stay curious.
